literature.headline_zh: 马尔堡病毒病在非洲重新出现。

key_findings_zh: 非洲多个地区近期检测到马尔堡病毒,表明其隐性循环范围扩大 [10.1080/22221751.2026.2728744]。

LIR-DP方法成功识别出马尔堡病毒核蛋白中的功能性LIR模体,有助于理解病毒如何利用自噬通路 [10.1371/journal.ppat.1014607]。
缺乏疫苗和抗病毒药物,支持性治疗仍是主要手段 [10.1128/cmr.00097-23]。

literature.headline_en: Re-emerging Marburg virus disease in Africa.
literature.lead_en: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is re-emerging across Africa, indicating broader enzootic circulation and ongoing spillover risks.
key_findings_en: Recent detections in multiple African regions suggest wider enzootic circulation than previously recognized [10.1080/22221751.2026.2728744]
Ecological suitability expansion and increased human activity raise spillover risks by increasing contact with Egyptian rousette bats [10.1080/22221751.2026.2728744]
Case fatality rates for MVD range widely, from 24% to 90%, highlighting its high mortality [10.1128/cmr.00097-23]
The LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) identified functional LIR motifs in the nucleoprotein of Marburg virus, offering insights into viral manipulation of autophagy [10.1371/journal.ppat.1014607]
Currently, there are no approved vaccines or antiviral treatments for MVD, with supportive care being the mainstay [10.1128/cmr.00097-23]
literature.trend_or_risk_en: The geographic spread and spillover risks of MVD are increasing, necessitating enhanced surveillance and preparedness.
literature.caveats_en: Some conclusions are based on computational predictions and in vitro experiments, requiring further in vivo validation.
literature.brief_en: Marburg virus disease is re-emerging in Africa, with evidence of broader circulation and increased spillover risks. The LIR-DP method has identified functional LIR motifs in viral proteins, providing insights into viral mechanisms. No approved vaccines or antiviral treatments exist, and supportive care remains the primary approach.

papers.title: Re-emerging Marburg virus disease in Africa: spillover ecology, geographic expansion, and surveillance vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is re-emerging across Africa as a high-consequence zoonosis shaped by expanding ecological suitability, repeated spillover, and uneven surveillance capacity. This review synthesizes current evidence on the ecological, epidemiological, and operational determinants of contemporary Marburg virus (MARV) emergence. We conceptualize MVD as an ecological-emergence system produced by interactions among reservoir-host biology, environmental change, human exposure, health-system readiness, and mobility, rather than as a series of isolated outbreaks. Recent detections in multiple African regions indicate wider enzootic circulation than previously recognized and support repeated, reservoir-associated introductions from distributed ecological foci. Spillover risk is heightened where mining, land-use change, agricultural encroachment, settlement growth, climate-sensitive habitat disruption, and population movement increase contact with Egyptian rousette bats ( Rousettus aegyptiacus ) and contaminated roost environments. Following primary spillover, diagnostic delays, fragmented surveillance, limited laboratory decentralization, healthcare-associated transmission, and mobility-linked exposure can enable outbreak amplification and delayed recognition. Serological findings further suggest possible "shadow epidemiology," with unrecognized or mild MARV infections occurring outside confirmed outbreak chains. Critical preparedness gaps persist in ecological risk mapping, longitudinal reservoir surveillance, decentralized molecular diagnostics, genomic sequencing, data integration, and cross-border early warning. Future preparedness should move beyond reactive containment toward integrated One Health approach combining predictive ecological surveillance, rapid community-level detection, real-time genomics, infection prevention, risk communication, and regional coordination to identify spillover early and prevent human transmission.

The analysis highlights the need for an integrated One Health approach to address the complex interactions between reservoir-host biology, environmental factors, human exposure, and health-system readiness. papers.title_zh: 非洲重新出现的马尔堡病毒病(MVD):跨物种溢出生态学、地理扩散及监测脆弱性
papers.source_body_en: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is re-emerging across Africa as a high-consequence zoonosis shaped by expanding ecological suitability, repeated spillover, and uneven surveillance capacity. This review synthesizes current evidence on the ecological, epidemiological, and operational determinants of contemporary Marburg virus (MARV) emergence. We conceptualize MVD as an ecological-emergence system produced by interactions among reservoir-host biology, environmental change, human exposure, health-system readiness, and mobility, rather than as a series of isolated outbreaks. Recent detections in multiple African regions indicate wider enzootic circulation than previously recognized and support repeated, reservoir-associated introductions from distributed ecological foci. Spillover risk is heightened where mining, land-use change, agricultural encroachment, settlement growth, climate-sensitive habitat disruption, and population movement increase contact with Egyptian rousette bats ( Rousettus aegyptiacus ) and contaminated roost environments. Following primary spillover, diagnostic delays, fragmented surveillance, limited laboratory decentralization, healthcare-associated transmission, and mobility-linked exposure can enable outbreak amplification and delayed recognition. Serological findings further suggest possible "shadow epidemiology," with unrecognized or mild MARV infections occurring outside confirmed outbreak chains. Critical preparedness gaps persist in ecological risk mapping, longitudinal reservoir surveillance, decentralized molecular diagnostics, genomic sequencing, data integration, and cross-border early warning. Future preparedness should move beyond reactive containment toward integrated One Health approach combining predictive ecological surveillance, rapid community-level detection, real-time genomics, infection prevention, risk communication, and regional coordination to identify spillover early and prevent human transmission.
papers.abstract_zh: 马尔堡病毒病(MVD)正在非洲重新出现,作为一种高后果性的人兽共患病,其流行受到生态适宜性扩展、反复的跨物种溢出以及不均衡的监测能力的影响。本综述总结了当前关于当代马尔堡病毒(MARV)出现的生态学、流行病学和操作性决定因素的证据。我们将MVD概念化为一个由储存宿主-宿主生物学、环境变化、人类暴露、卫生系统准备度和流动性相互作用所产生的生态性出现系统,而非一系列孤立的暴发。在多个非洲地区近期的检测结果表明,其隐性循环范围比之前认为的更广,并支持了来自分散生态焦点的反复、与储存宿主相关的引入。在采矿、土地利用变化、农业扩张、聚居地增长、气候敏感性栖息地破坏和人口流动增加导致与埃及 rousette 蝙蝠(Rousettus aegyptiacus)及污染栖息地接触的地区,跨物种溢出风险显著升高。在初次跨物种溢出后,诊断延迟、碎片化的监测、实验室资源分散、与医疗相关的传播以及与流动性相关的暴露可能促进暴发的放大和延迟识别。血清学发现进一步表明可能存在未被识别或轻微的MARV感染,这些感染发生在确认的暴发传播链之外。在生态风险图谱、纵向储存宿主 监测、分散式分子诊断、基因组测序、数据整合和跨境早期预警方面,关键的准备缺口仍然存在。未来应超越被动防控,转向整合的One Health方法,结合预测性生态监测、快速社区级检测、实时基因组学、感染预防、风险沟通和区域协调,以早期识别跨物种溢出并防止人类传播。

papers.title: Marburg virus disease: a comprehensive review
papers.abstract: SUMMARY Marburg virus disease (MVD) is a highly fatal illness closely resembling Ebola disease, caused by either Marburg virus (MARV) or Ravn virus (RAVV). It typically begins with a sudden onset of high fever, headache, and malaise, followed by severe gastrointestinal symptoms, bleeding disorders, and, in the most severe cases, multi-organ failure. Case fatality rates vary widely, from 24% up to 90%. MARV and RAVV are zoonotic pathogens, with fruit bats recognized as the main reservoir. Human-to-human transmission generally occurs through direct exposure to infected bodily fluids. Historically, MVD outbreaks were primarily restricted to Central and Eastern Africa. In recent years, however, the disease has appeared in new regions: Ghana recorded its first cases in 2022, followed by concurrent outbreaks in Equatorial Guinea and Tanzania in 2023. Rwanda and Ethiopia experienced their debut outbreaks in 2024 and 2025, respectively, and another outbreak occurred in early 2025 in Tanzania. These incidents point to a troubling rise in annual MVD outbreaks and emphasize the ongoing risk of spillover from wildlife reservoirs and continued human-to-human transmission. papers.title: Discovering host-viral protein interactions in autophagy: A LIR discovery pipeline for identifying LC3-interacting region motifs in highly virulent viruses.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever virus (HFV) infections are highly fatal, posing a significant global pandemic threat as they continue to emerge in new locations. HFVs and other highly virulent viruses (HVVs), such as Nipah virus, exploit host cell pathways, including the conserved host autophagy pathway, to promote viral replication. The Atg8/microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) proteins are necessary for autophagosome formation and maturation. Proteins interact with Atg8-family proteins through LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs, which is a short linear motif (SLiM) found in intrinsically disordered regions of proteins. The presence of these motifs in viral components suggests they play a role in hijacking or evading the host autophagy pathway, yet the identification of functional LIR motifs in viral proteins remains limited. To address this gap, we developed the LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) which integrates amino acid sequence pattern matching, with protein disorder prediction using IUPred3, and modeling with AlphaFold3. Using LIR-DP, we identified 43 putative LIR motifs in 166 proteins from 22 HVVs and predicted that 18 of these LIRs would be functional. In vitro and in cellulo laboratory experiments demonstrated that LIRs from the Marburg virus nucleoprotein, the Nipah virus phosphoprotein, the Ebola virus VP35, and the Rift Valley fever virus NSs protein bind to Atg8/LC3 family proteins. The aromatic amino acid in the first position of each LIR motif was found to be critical for these interactions. We provide evidence for the utility of the LIR-DP in identifying functional LIRs within HVV proteins which may provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which HVVs modulate the autophagy pathway during infection.

papers.title_zh: 发现宿主病毒蛋白在自噬中的相互作用:一种用于识别高致病性病毒中LC3相互作用区域模体的LIR发现流程。
papers.source_body_en: Hemorrhagic fever virus (HFV) infections are highly fatal, posing a significant global pandemic threat as they continue to emerge in new locations. HFVs and other highly virulent viruses (HVVs), such as Nipah virus, exploit host cell pathways, including the conserved host autophagy pathway, to promote viral replication. The Atg8/microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) proteins are necessary for autophagosome formation and maturation. Proteins interact with Atg8-family proteins through LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs, which is a short linear motif (SLiM) found in intrinsically disordered regions of proteins. The presence of these motifs in viral components suggests they play a role in hijacking or evading the host autophagy pathway, yet the identification of functional LIR motifs in viral proteins remains limited. To address this gap, we developed the LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) which integrates amino acid sequence pattern matching, with protein disorder prediction using IUPred3, and modeling with AlphaFold3. Using LIR-DP, we identified 43 putative LIR motifs in 166 proteins from 22 HVVs and predicted that 18 of these LIRs would be functional. In vitro and in cellulo laboratory experiments demonstrated that LIRs from the Marburg virus nucleoprotein, the Nipah virus phosphoprotein, the Ebola virus VP35, and the Rift Valley fever virus NSs protein bind to Atg8/LC3 family proteins. The aromatic amino acid in the first position of each LIR motif was found to be critical for these interactions. We provide evidence for the utility of the LIR-DP in identifying functional LIRs within HVV proteins which may provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which HVVs modulate the autophagy pathway during infection.
papers.abstract_zh: 出血热病毒(HFV)感染具有高度致命性,随着其不断在新地区出现,构成了重大的全球大流行威胁。HFV和其他高致病性病毒(HVVs),如尼帕病毒,利用宿主细胞通路,包括保守的宿主自噬通路,以促进病毒复制。Atg8/微管相关蛋白1轻链3(LC3)蛋白对于自噬体的形成和成熟是必需的。蛋白质通过LC3相互作用区域(LIR)模体与Atg8家族蛋白相互作用,这种模体是一种存在于蛋白质内禀无序区域中的短线性模体(SLiM)。这些模体在病毒组分中的存在表明它们可能在劫持或逃避宿主自噬通路中发挥作用,但目前在病毒蛋白中识别功能性LIR模体仍存在局限。为了解决这一问题,我们开发了LIR发现流程(LIR-DP),该流程整合了氨基酸序列模式匹配、使用IUPred3进行蛋白质无序预测以及使用AlphaFold3进行建模。通过LIR-DP,我们在22种高致病性病毒(HVVs)的166个蛋白质中识别出43个潜在的LIR模体,并预测其中18个为功能性。体外和细胞内实验表明,来自马尔堡病毒核蛋白、尼帕病毒磷酸蛋白、埃博拉病毒VP35以及裂谷热病毒NSs蛋白的LIR模体能够与Atg8/LC3家族蛋白结合。每个LIR模体的第一个芳香族氨基酸被发现对这些相互作用至关重要。我们提供了LIR-DP在识别高致病性病毒(HVVs)蛋白中的功能性LIR模体方面的有效性证据,这可能为理解HVVs在感染期间如何调节自噬通路提供有价值的见解。

Ebola Disease: Current Situation CDC is monitoring an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Learn more: Ebola Outbreak: Current Situation. For travelers returning to the United States from DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan, visit: Information for Travelers Returning from Ebola-Affected Areas. At a glance CDC established an office in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2002. CDC collaborates closely with the Government of DRC, the Ministry of Health (MOH), and various partners to build effective public health collaboration and partnerships to detect, prevent, and respond to global public health threats. CDC's work aims to protect the health of Americans and support public health around the world. Key accomplishments Pioneering electronic integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) using the DHIS2 platform in six provinces, allowing real-time surveillance reporting with integrated laboratory results, to improve the 7-1-7 model for outbreak responses in the DRC. Mentored 16 laboratories towards ISO 15189 accreditation, including two that became DRC’s first internationally accredited clinical laboratories in 2025. Established diagnostic capacities for HIV, monkeypox, and viral hemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Marburg Virus Disease and Ebola), and supported installation of a lab information system in 10 laboratories to streamline operations. Supported the training of 925 disease detectives through the Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), trained 120 MOH staff in emergency management, and educated over 3,800 healthcare providers in malaria diagnosis and treatment. Deployed staff and lab equipment to the 2025 Ebola outbreak (16th Ebola outbreak in DRC) in Bulape to support surveillance and laboratory testing. Supported the Ebola Treatment Unit laboratory to perform specimen testing for patient follow up. Provided technical support for surveillance and tetanus vaccination campaigns that led to the elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus in 2019. Contributed to the recent monkeypox and Ebola responses through laboratory testing, case investigations, infection prevention and control, risk communication, and community engagement. Global health security The Ministry of Health works with healthcare workers to monitor contacts of people diagnosed with Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak. SOURCE: Photo by Mary Claire Worrell/CDC DRC has a large population, spans a vast geographic area, and shares borders with nine other countries. CDC, MOH, and various partners collaborate to prevent, detect, respond to, and control infectious disease outbreaks within the country. CDC was the major partner who worked with the MOH to establish the National Public Health Institute (NPHI) in 2022, which coordinates essential public health functions such as preparedness and outbreak response, surveillance, laboratory systems, and workforce development. Laboratory strengthening CDC has successfully accredited two laboratories to ISO 15189 standards. Additionally, CDC helped develop a national laboratory strategic plan that directs the strengthening of laboratory systems in DRC. This includes donating essential equipment and enhancing laboratory diagnostics, network optimization, and quality management systems to meet the growing demand for early diagnosis of infectious diseases. CDC also supported the installation of a laboratory information system (LIS) in 10 laboratories to streamline their processes. Furthermore, CDC has provided training for laboratory staff and monitored testing quality through an external quality assurance program. Workforce development DRC’s FETP currently offers three levels of training: frontline, intermediate, and advanced. Participants enhance their skills in data collection and the translation of data into evidence-based actions. FETP graduates primarily include national and district public health staff, whose expertise has been vital in DRC’s responses to monkeypox, Ebola, COVID-19, and cholera. CDC has supported more than 900 FETP deployers throughout the country to participate in polio surveillance, monkeypox and Ebola outbreak responses, vaccination campaigns, and other immunization activities. Through FETP, CDC strengthens DRC’s workforce capacity to identify and contain outbreaks before they escalate globally. Ebola 2026 Ebola Outbreak: What CDC is Doing CDC is working with international partners on this evolving situation. CDC has taken proactive measures to prevent Ebola from entering the United States. To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Learn more about CDC's efforts CDC has supported Ebola outbreak responses through disease surveillance, laboratory support, border health, data management, infection prevention and control, vaccination, and risk communication and community engagement. For DRC’s 2025 Ebola outbreak in Bulape, CDC-supported activities included: Deploying a mobile sequencing laboratory to perform real-time data that links cases and guides response activities. Sending 27 field epidemiologists to assist with case investigations and contact-tracing. Additionally, CDC headquarters subject matter experts and CDC DRC Country Office staff have deployed to Bulape to provide technical assistance for the response. Digitalizing and harmonizing data by deploying and expanding the DHIS2 in Kasai and neighboring provinces to enhance real time data reporting and analysis. Aug 12, 2026 Monkeypox CDC has provided support for monkeypox research and response in DRC for over 20 years. DRC declared a monkeypox outbreak in 2022, which was classified as a public health emergency of international concern in August 2024. As of October 2025, the country has reported approximately 100,000 monkeypox cases. CDC is actively assisting the MOH with the response including surveillance, laboratory capacity, and workforce. The deployment of 50 to 70 field epidemiologists in hotspot provinces has been instrumental in mitigating the outbreak. CDC collaborated to assess the effectiveness of the monkeypox vaccine (MBA-BN), used in an endemic zone in 1,600 health care workers in 6 health zones of Tshuapa province. The study showed an effective antibody response in 99% of recipients for up to 5 years. Keep Reading Clade I Monkeypox Outbreaks HIV and TB As a key implementer of the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), CDC plays an essential role in the fight against HIV and TB. With unmatched scientific and technical knowledge and long-standing relationships with ministries of health, CDC is uniquely positioned to advance HIV, TB, and other global health security activities that keep Americans safe at home and abroad. Through PEPFAR, CDC provides critical support to DRC's public health infrastructure, improving the country's ability to prevent, detect, and respond to HIV, TB, and other infectious diseases and minimizing their risk from entering the U.S. For Public Health HIV and TB Overview: Democratic Republic of the Congo Immunization CDC supports the MOH in the distribution and mass vaccination campaigns for new vaccines. CDC also works to improve outbreak detection, and enhance disease surveillance systems and reduce their impact on human health and economies. CDC’s immunization-related support to DRC reduces the burden of vaccine-preventable diseases and lowers the risk of disease transmission beyond the country’s borders, thereby protecting the U.S. and safeguarding Americans. Cholera DRC continues to experience cholera outbreaks, driven by poor sanitation, limited access to clean water, and ongoing conflict. CDC provides technical assistance to MOH, focusing on improving surveillance, outbreak response, and laboratory capacities. Additionally, CDC has funded a partner to implement essential water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) initiatives aimed at reducing cholera transmission by enhancing access to safe drinking water, promoting hygiene practices, and ensuring adequate sanitation facilities for vulnerable populations. Malaria CDC has collaborated with partners to support implementation of malaria prevention and control activities in DRC. CDC-supported activities have included providing technical input in: Monitoring mosquito behavior and resistance to insecticides. Providing long-lasting insecticide-treated bed nets. Preventing malaria during pregnancy. Enhancing diagnostics, surveillance, and evaluation of malaria-related activities. Researching social and behavioral changes impacting malaria prevention and case management. Influenza With financial and technical support from CDC, DRC began influenza surveillance in 2006. Currently, four sentinel sites conduct influenza surveillance in DRC's capital of Kinshasa. Influenza surveillance is focused among patients with influenza-like illness or severe acute respiratory illness. These activities formed the backbone for conducting COVID-19 surveillance in DRC. Mar 18, 2026 Download Download Success story spotlight Strengthening Health Screening at Airports to Curb Ebola Spread CDC DRC Senior Surveillance Specialist Dr. Joelle Kabamba helped ensure that the handwashing stations at N’djili International Airport were working. The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the largest ever reported in the country and the second largest Ebola outbreak ever. Because there are no approved vaccines or treatments for the type of Ebola virus causing the outbreak, early detection and rapid isolation of ill people are vital to saving lives. Airports, land borders, and river crossings are important checkpoints for detecting potential illnesses and preventing diseases like Ebola from spreading across borders. CDC is providing technical support to DRC's government to strengthen public health screening for Ebola at N'djili International Airport, the country's largest airport, as well as other key points of entry. CDC experts are assessing departure and arrival operations, infection prevention and control practices, and procedures for identifying and reporting sick travelers. They are also providing practical recommendations to strengthen screeners' ability to identify, isolate, and report ill travelers. This work helps local border health staff detect and isolate suspected Ebola cases among travelers and get them the help they need. Trained personnel, standardized procedures, and faster reporting increase the likelihood of identifying and isolating sick individuals before they travel. By improving the odds of identifying suspected Ebola cases and responding quickly, CDC helps safeguard the health of Americans and communities worldwide. This work not only strengthens the current Ebola response but also enhances preparedness and resilience for future public health emergencies. - Dr. Joelle Kabamba Success stories Another Battle Won Against Ebola CDC helped the Democratic Republic of the Congo contain its 16th Ebola outbreak, saving lives. DRC declared a monkeypox outbreak in 2022, which was classified as a public health emergency of international concern in August 2024. As of October 2025, the country has reported approximately 100,000 monkeypox cases. CDC is actively assisting the MOH with the response including surveillance, laboratory capacity, and workforce. The deployment of 50 to 70 field epidemiologists in hotspot provinces has been instrumental in mitigating the outbreak. CDC collaborated to assess the effectiveness of the monkeypox vaccine (MBA-BN), used in an endemic zone in 1,600 health care workers in 6 health zones of Tshuapa province. CDC’s immunization-related support to DRC reduces the burden of vaccine-preventable diseases and lowers the risk of disease transmission beyond the country’s borders, thereby protecting the U.S. and safeguarding Americans. Cholera DRC continues to experience cholera outbreaks, driven by poor sanitation, limited access to clean water, and ongoing conflict. CDC provides technical assistance to MOH, focusing on improving surveillance, outbreak response, and laboratory capacities. Additionally, CDC has funded a partner to implement essential water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) initiatives aimed at reducing cholera transmission by enhancing access to safe drinking water, promoting hygiene practices, and ensuring adequate sanitation facilities for vulnerable populations. Malaria CDC has collaborated with partners to support implementation of malaria prevention and control activities in DRC. The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the largest ever reported in the country and the second largest Ebola outbreak ever. Because there are no approved vaccines or treatments for the type of Ebola virus causing the outbreak, early detection and rapid isolation of ill people are vital to saving lives. Airports, land borders, and river crossings are important checkpoints for detecting potential illnesses and preventing diseases like Ebola from spreading across borders. CDC is providing technical support to DRC's government to strengthen public health screening for Ebola at N'djili International Airport, the country's largest airport, as well as other key points of entry. CDC experts are assessing departure and arrival operations, infection prevention and control practices, and procedures for identifying and reporting sick travelers. They are also providing practical recommendations to strengthen screeners' ability to identify, isolate, and report ill travelers. This work helps local border health staff detect and isolate suspected Ebola cases among travelers and get them the help they need. Trained personnel, standardized procedures, and faster reporting increase the likelihood of identifying and isolating sick individuals before they travel. By improving the odds of identifying suspected Ebola cases and responding quickly, CDC helps safeguard the health of Americans and communities worldwide. Outbreaks You Never Heard About: CDC Experts on the Frontlines (World Field Epidemiology Day) View LargerDownload CDC's global health security experts are on the frontlines stopping deadly threats before they can spread in the U.S. View LargerDownload CDC's global health security experts are on the frontlines stopping deadly threats before they can spread in the U.S. View LargerDownload In 2025, CDC's global health security experts and Senegalese health officials rapidly contained a deadly outbreak of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, stopping it at the source before it could cross borders. View LargerDownload In 2024, when an American man returned to Iowa from Liberia unknowingly infected with Lassa fever, CDC experts acted fast to safeguard Americans from the threat, containing it before it could spread. View LargerDownload In 2025, global health experts, including CDC-trained disease detectives partnered with Ethiopian health officials to detect and contain Ethiopia's very first Marburg virus outbreak, before it could reach the United States. View LargerDownload In 2023, CDC's global health security experts and country partners identified the source of a mystery neurological illness, Guillain-Barré syndrome, in Guatemala and quickly contained the spread before it could cross borders. View LargerDownload In Nigeria, a CDC-trained disease detective used innovative post-mortem surveillance to uncover hidden Lassa fever and dengue cases—helping stop threats before they could spread farther and put Americans at risk. Outbreaks You Never Heard About: Because CDC Was There View LargerDownload Every day, CDC's global health security experts are on the frontlines helping to stop outbreaks before they spread and reach the U.S.—American-led global health security in action, keeping Americans safe. View LargerDownload In 2025, CDC experts and local partners in Vietnam contained a potentially deadly outbreak, moving the situation from crisis to control and helping protect U.S. travelers. View LargerDownload In Uganda, CDC-trained experts quickly investigated and contained an Ebola outbreak—before it could cross borders—an example of American-led global health security helping keep Americans safe. View LargerDownload Early detection in Tanzania helped stop and detect a deadly Marburg outbreak from crisis to control, demonstrating how CDC’s work helps protect Americans. View LargerDownload Thanks to CDC-trained disease detectives, DRC was able to dramatically turn the tide on an Ebola outbreak—American-led global health security in action, stopping threats at their source and keeping Americans safe. Global Health Security Conference View LargerDownload Global Health Security Conference 2026 View LargerDownload At #GHS2026, CDC new findings show that investments in global health security helped contain 10 Ebola outbreaks across Sub-Saharan Africa (2016-2023) - saving billions and delivering more than $4 for every $1 invested. View LargerDownload At #GHS2026, CDC experts highlight how data-driven approaches are improving outbreak detection and response. View LargerDownload New CDC findings at #GHS2026 show how rapid response teams helped strengthen Sierra Leone's monkeypox response, improving coordination and reducing cases through faster detection. View LargerDownload At #GHS2026, CDC experts showcase how laboratory science is helping to track drug-resistant bacteria in hospitals in Vietnam. International Day of Epidemic Preparedness View LargerDownload It is essential to highlight the urgent need to invest in systems that can prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease outbreaks. View LargerDownload It is essential to highlight the urgent need to invest in systems that can prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease outbreaks. Download CDC’s preparedness efforts in Vietnam are helping that country detect viruses faster. Download CDC’s partnership with Sierra Leone in using 7-1-7 has enabled this country to make significant strides in strengthening its public health systems needed for response. World Health Workers Week View LargerDownload Every April, CDC celebrates the remarkable contributions of global public health workers dedicated to safeguarding and strengthening health security worldwide. View LargerDownload CDC-trained community health worker Vedestina Shumbusho’s swift actions helped stem a recent Marburg virus outbreak in Tanzania. View LargerDownload A graduate of the CDC-supported FETP Frontline program in Colombia, Esteban Arpushana is a leader in bilingual health advocacy and pioneering community-based interventions. View LargerDownload Fhatuwani Gavhi, MPH, an epidemiologist at CDC's Division of Global Health Protection is a leading force in strengthening South Africa’s epidemic preparedness. View LargerDownload CDC's Program Director for the Division of Global Health Protection in Vietnam, Lindsay Kim, MD, MPH is advancing laboratory capabilities for global health security in Vietnam. View LargerDownload A behavioral scientist who joined CDC’s response team in Zambia, Christina Craig, MSc played a pivotal role in combating Zambia’s cholera outbreak. Submit Our latest issue Outbreaks You Never Heard About: CDC Experts on the Frontlines CDC's global health security experts are on the frontlines stopping deadly threats before they can spread in the U.S. A health threat overseas can reach U.S. communities in just 36 hours. Yet many outbreaks never make headlines because CDC’s global health security experts are on the frontlines, helping detect and contain dangerous diseases before they spread farther or threaten Americans. In the past two years alone, these experts have helped contain more than 250 outbreaks across 40+ countries, from Marburg and other hemorrhagic fevers to dengue and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Today, that work includes CDC teams on the ground in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, working alongside partners to help stop the current Ebola outbreak at its source. Based overseas and at CDC headquarters, these teams form a critical part of CDC’s global health security work, helping ensure continued U.S. leadership in protecting our nation’s security. In recognition of World Field Epidemiology Day, the “Outbreaks You Never Heard About” campaign spotlights CDC-trained disease detectives and the crucial role they play in that work: finding cases, tracing how diseases spread, and turning data into action. Since 1980, CDC’s landmark Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP) has trained more than 25,000 disease detectives in over 100 countries, strengthening the first line of defense against global health threats and helping protect American lives, livelihoods, and health security here at home. For Public Health World Field Epidemiology Day Deadly Outbreak: Stopped in Senegal In 2025, CDC's global health security experts and Senegalese health officials rapidly contained a deadly outbreak of Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever, stopping it at the source before it could cross borders. In 2025, Senegal faced an outbreak of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a deadly disease that can spread between people and animals. CDC-trained disease detectives joined CDC global health security and technical experts and country partners to quickly trace contacts and test human and animal samples, helping contain the outbreak in just two weeks and prevent further spread. For Public Health World Field Epidemiology Day Lassa Fever: Stopped in Its Tracks In 2024, when an American man returned to Iowa from Liberia unknowingly infected with Lassa fever, CDC experts acted fast to safeguard Americans from the threat, containing it before it could spread. In 2024, a U.S. traveler returned from Liberia with Lassa fever, a potentially deadly virus. Drawing on 16 years of CDC’s work strengthening disease detection and response in Liberia, CDC experts quickly provided Iowa health officials with laboratory testing, contact tracing, and infection prevention support—helping prevent spread in the United States. For Public Health World Field Epidemiology Day Deadly Marburg Outbreak Stopped Before It Spread In 2025, global health experts, including CDC-trained disease detectives partnered with Ethiopian health officials to detect and contain Ethiopia's very first Marburg virus outbreak, before it could reach the United States. When Marburg virus surfaced in Ethiopia for the first time, CDC experts and trained Ethiopian disease detectives moved quickly to investigate cases, strengthen surveillance, and support border health measures—helping contain the outbreak before it spread farther or reached the United States. For Public Health World Field Epidemiology Day Mystery Illness Quickly Solved in Major Travel Route In 2023, CDC's global health security experts and country partners identified the source of a mystery neurological illness, Guillain-Barré Syndrome, in Guatemala and quickly contained the spread before it could cross borders. In late 2023, a cluster of severe neurological illness emerged along Guatemala’s Pan-American Highway. CDC experts and local partners identified a likely foodborne cause within one month and contained the outbreak within three months—preventing further spread along a major travel corridor to the United States. For Public Health World Field Epidemiology Day Hidden Threat Uncovered Thanks to CDC-Trained Expert In Nigeria, a CDC-trained disease detective used innovative post-mortem surveillance to uncover hidden Lassa fever and dengue cases—helping stop threats before they could spread farther and put Americans at risk. In northwest Nigeria, a CDC-trained disease detective helped uncover 11 previously undetected Lassa fever infections and one dengue infection through an innovative post-mortem surveillance system—giving health officials critical information to identify the hidden threats and prevent their spread across borders. For Public Health World Field Epidemiology Day Where we work Learn more about how CDC works to protect public health around the world: Our Global Presence CDC has a network of country and regional offices in over 60 countries.
